Three Famous Food Markets in Europe: Shop, Eat and Tip

Quality checked lesson

Visit three famous European food markets in Barcelona, Paris and London. Learn what you can find there, then practise the English you need to choose food, check ingredients, pay and tip.

Before You Start

Think about these questions.

  1. What food do you like to buy at a market?

    Need a starting line?

    Helpful clue: You can name fruit, bread, cheese, a snack or another food.

  2. Which city would you like to visit: Barcelona, Paris or London?

    Need a starting line?

    Helpful clue: Choose one city and give one simple reason.

  3. What do you check before you buy unfamiliar food?

    Need a starting line?

    Helpful clue: Think about the price, ingredients, amount or payment.

Typing practice

Type the text exactly. Timer starts with your first key.

Text to type: La Boqueria is on La Rambla, a famous street in Barcelona. More than 200 traders work in the market. They sell fruit, vegetables, fish, meat, cheese, nuts, olives and other groceries. There are also bars where visitors can eat. The many bright stalls make the market exciting, but it is useful to stop and look before buying. Common short questions are “What is popular here?” and “Is this local?” Some food is sold by weight. The order “Two hundred grams, please” gives an exact amount. Payment can be different at each stall, so “Do you take cards?” checks the payment method early.

Typing practice

Type the text exactly. Timer starts with your first key.

Text to type: Tipping is different in Spain, France and the UK. In Spain, a tip is optional. Some people round up the bill, but customers do not always add money. In France, service is normally included in the restaurant price, so the question “Is service included?” confirms the situation. An extra tip is optional. In the UK, the bill may show a discretionary or compulsory service charge. The question “Is there a service charge?” makes an unclear bill easier to understand. At a simple food counter, “Do I need to leave a tip?” is polite and helps a visitor avoid paying twice.

Roleplay 2: Ask About a Nut Allergy

Cook

Hello. Would you like this rice dish?

You

What is in this?

Cook

The practice ingredient card lists rice, chicken, vegetables and almonds.

You

Does this contain nuts? I am allergic to nuts.

Cook

Yes. It contains almonds, and other food here may also touch nuts.

You

Then I will not eat the dish. One of these sealed waters, please.

Cook

Of course. Here is one sealed water.

You

Thank you for the clear answer.

Cook

You are welcome. Your order is complete.

Roleplay 3: Order and Pay in London

Counter Worker

Hello. What would you like?

You

One cheese toastie, please. Do you take cards?

Counter Worker

Yes, this practice counter takes cards. The toastie is seven pounds.

You

Is there a service charge?

Counter Worker

No. This fictional bill has no service charge.

You

Do I need to leave a tip?

Counter Worker

No, not in this exercise. In the UK, always read the bill because it may show a service charge.

You

Thank you. I will pay seven pounds by card.

Speak

Your Turn: Three Market Orders

Speak through each situation. Use the phrases from the lesson.

  1. At La Boqueria, ask about local olives, order 200 grams and check card payment.

    Need a starting line?

    Start with: What is popular here?

    Helpful clue: Ask what is popular and local, give the amount, then ask whether the seller takes cards.

  2. At Marché des Enfants Rouges, ask about a dish and explain a nut allergy.

    Need a starting line?

    Start with: What is in this?

    Helpful clue: Ask about ingredients and nuts, state the allergy, then choose or refuse the food.

  3. At Borough Market, order lunch and check whether you need to add money for service.

    Need a starting line?

    Start with: One cheese toastie, please.

    Helpful clue: Order, ask about a service charge, then ask whether you need to leave a tip.

Reading

La Boqueria: Colour and Choice in Barcelona

La Boqueria is on La Rambla, a famous street in Barcelona.

More than 200 traders work in the market.

They sell fruit, vegetables, fish, meat, cheese, nuts, olives and other groceries.

There are also bars where visitors can eat.

The many bright stalls make the market exciting, but it is useful to stop and look before buying.

Common short questions are “What is popular here?”

and “Is this local?”

Some food is sold by weight.

The order “Two hundred grams, please” gives an exact amount.

Payment can be different at each stall, so “Do you take cards?”

checks the payment method early.

Reading

Marché des Enfants Rouges: Old Paris, Many Flavours

Marché des Enfants Rouges is a covered market in Paris.

It opened in 1615 and is the oldest food market in the city.

Traders sell fresh food, and small counters serve prepared dishes from different food cultures.

You may see vegetables and cheese, then choose a hot lunch nearby.

This variety is interesting, but an unfamiliar dish may have ingredients you cannot see.

The questions “What is in this?”

and “Does this contain nuts?”

make the problem clear.

The statement “I am allergic to nuts” gives important information.

After a suitable choice, “One of these, please” completes the order.

Reading

Borough Market: Produce and Street Food in London

Borough Market is a large food market in London with more than 100 businesses.

Its traders include bakers, cheese sellers, fish sellers, and fruit and vegetable sellers.

Visitors can shop for ingredients or go to Borough Market Kitchen for street food.

This makes the market a place for both shopping and lunch.

First, walk around and compare a few stalls.

Look at the food and the displayed price.

When you are ready, order at the counter and listen for the total.

A busy stall may move quickly, so keep your order short.

Before paying, check whether the counter accepts your preferred payment method.

Reading

Tipping in Spain, France and the UK

Tipping is different in Spain, France and the UK.

In Spain, a tip is optional.

Some people round up the bill, but customers do not always add money.

In France, service is normally included in the restaurant price, so the question “Is service included?”

confirms the situation.

An extra tip is optional.

In the UK, the bill may show a discretionary or compulsory service charge.

The question “Is there a service charge?”

makes an unclear bill easier to understand.

At a simple food counter, “Do I need to leave a tip?”

is polite and helps a visitor avoid paying twice.
